It takes no seed argument; to get a reproducible sequence for testing you call the separate `setseed(value)` function first, rather than passing a seed to `random()` itself.

questions.prompt: Why does inserting the literal 'don''t' (with two single quotes) store the text don't (with one apostrophe)?

choices.text: Two adjacent literals 'don' and 't' are joined into one
Inside a single-quoted literal, '' is the escape for one quote
The second quote is dropped as a typo, with a warning
It is invalid unless standard_conforming_strings is off

query.title: Escaping quotes inside string literals
query.syntax:
SELECT 'don''t';  -- don't
SELECT E'don\'t'; -- also don't, using an escape string literal
query.explanation: The SQL standard (and Postgres by default) escapes an embedded single quote inside a plain string literal by doubling it, not with a backslash. Backslash escapes only work inside an `E'...'` "escape string" literal, and are not honored in a plain string unless the `standard_conforming_strings` setting has been turned off, which is not the modern default.

questions.prompt: users.email is stored in lower case and has a B-tree index. Which query finds a user by email faster?

choices.text: Compare email directly
choices.code: SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = 'user4242@example.com'

choices.text: Compare lower(email)
choices.code: SELECT id FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user4242@example.com'
choices.rationale: An index on email cannot answer a condition on lower(email), so the planner scans every row and calls lower() on each.

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 50,000-row table.
criterion.evidence: A: 0.002 ms, B: 3.4 ms median on PostgreSQL 17.11

query.title: Functions on indexed columns hide the index
query.explanation: A B-tree index on `email` stores `email` values, not `lower(email)` values, so a condition on the expression cannot use it. Compare the column itself, or create an expression index on `lower(email)` if case-insensitive lookups are needed.

questions.prompt: Which query checks faster whether customer 7 has any orders? (orders has 100,000 rows and no index on customer_id.)

choices.text: count(*) > 0
choices.code: SELECT count(*) > 0 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7
choices.rationale: count(*) has to read every matching row to finish the count, which means scanning the whole table.

choices.text: EXISTS
choices.code: SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7)

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 100,000-row table.
criterion.evidence: A: 2.3 ms, B: 0.002 ms median on PostgreSQL 17.11

query.title: Existence tests and subquery execution in Postgres
query.explanation: To answer "is there at least one?", `EXISTS` can stop as soon as it finds a row. `count(*)` must find every matching row before it can compare the count with zero.
query.syntax:
-- General forms for "are there any matching rows?"
--   EXISTS (subquery)            -> boolean
--   expr IN (subquery)           -> boolean
--   count(*) over matching rows  -> integer (aggregate)

-- Example 1: EXISTS as a scalar value
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoices WHERE account_id = 42);

-- Example 2: EXISTS in a WHERE clause (semi-join)
SELECT a.id
FROM accounts a
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoices i WHERE i.account_id = a.id);

-- Example 3: aggregate form, compared to a number
SELECT count(*) >= 1 FROM invoices WHERE account_id = 42;

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * EXISTS only cares whether the subquery returns at least one row;
--   the select list is ignored (SELECT 1 and SELECT * behave the same).
-- * The docs say the subquery is evaluated only far enough to
--   determine whether any row is returned.
-- * An aggregate like count(*) must consume all rows that its input
--   produces before it can return a value.
-- * NOT EXISTS is the usual way to test for absence.
-- * Compare plans with: EXPLAIN ANALYZE <query>;
-- * An index on the filtered column changes the scan type,
--   which affects how much work each form does.
-- * EXISTS never yields NULL; NOT IN can behave surprisingly with NULLs.

questions.prompt: products.id is the primary key. Which query fetches product 4242 faster?

choices.text: Compare id as an integer
choices.code: SELECT sku FROM products WHERE id = 4242

choices.text: Cast id to text
choices.code: SELECT sku FROM products WHERE id::text = '4242'
choices.rationale: Casting the column to text means the primary key index on id no longer applies, so every row is cast and compared.

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 50,000-row table.
criterion.evidence: A: 0.002 ms, B: 1.9 ms median on PostgreSQL 17.11

query.title: Index usage and WHERE clause expressions
query.explanation: An index can only serve a condition on the indexed column itself. `id::text = ...` applies a cast to every row. Compare `id` with an integer, casting the literal or parameter if needed, and the primary key index finds the row directly.
query.syntax:
-- General form: a B-tree index on a column can be used when the
-- WHERE condition compares the bare indexed column to a value
--   WHERE <indexed_column> <operator> <value>

-- Example setup
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_no bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  email    text
);
CREATE INDEX orders_email_idx ON orders (email);

-- Condition on the bare column
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE email = 'a@example.com';

-- Condition wraps the column in a function or cast
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE lower(email) = 'a@example.com';

-- Gotchas (as comments):
-- * An index stores the column's values. A condition on an expression
--   of the column (function call, cast, arithmetic) does not match
--   a plain index on that column.
-- * Expression index: CREATE INDEX ON orders (lower(email));
--   It matches queries that use the same expression.
-- * Constants can be cast instead: compare the column to a value
--   of the column's own type.
-- * Use EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) to see Index Scan vs Seq Scan.
-- * The planner may still pick a Seq Scan on tiny tables.

questions.prompt: products.sku has a B-tree index (C collation). Which query finds SKUs starting with SKU-0042 faster?

choices.text: left(sku, 8) = 'SKU-0042'
choices.code: SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE left(sku, 8) = 'SKU-0042'
choices.rationale: left(sku, 8) is an expression the index does not store, so every row is read and trimmed.

choices.text: sku LIKE 'SKU-0042%'
choices.code: SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE sku LIKE 'SKU-0042%'

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 50,000-row table.
criterion.evidence: A: 3.2 ms, B: 0.016 ms median on PostgreSQL 17.11

query.title: B-tree indexes and sargable predicates
query.explanation: With the C collation (or a `text_pattern_ops` index), Postgres turns `LIKE 'prefix%'` into a range condition on the index. Wrapping the column in `left()` or `substr()` gives the same answer but forces a scan of every row.
query.syntax:
-- General form: a B-tree index can be used when the WHERE clause
-- compares the indexed column itself (not a function of it) using
-- an operator the index supports.
--   WHERE indexed_col <op> constant

CREATE INDEX idx_users_name ON users (name);          -- default opclass
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_pat ON users (name text_pattern_ops); -- for LIKE in non-C locales

-- Example: range on the bare column
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name >= 'Bob' AND name < 'Boc';

-- Example: wrapping the column in a function hides it from the plain index
SELECT * FROM users WHERE upper(name) = 'BOB';        -- plain index on name not usable
CREATE INDEX idx_users_upper ON users (upper(name));  -- expression index fixes this

-- Gotchas:
-- * LIKE 'abc%' (constant prefix, no leading wildcard) can be turned into
--   a range scan on a B-tree, but only if the index collation is C,
--   or the index uses text_pattern_ops / varchar_pattern_ops.
-- * LIKE '%abc' (leading wildcard) cannot use a B-tree; consider pg_trgm GIN/GiST.
-- * An expression index is only used when the query contains the same expression.
-- * Check with: EXPLAIN SELECT ...;  look for Index Scan vs Seq Scan.
-- * Tiny tables may still use Seq Scan because the planner judges it cheaper.
